nodes.statement: (ii) The fact that $z_{G}$ is both a morphism and a comorphism of sites $((G\downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})\to ((1_{\hat{\cal D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}} )$ inducing equivalences making the diagram in the statement of the theorem commute follows from the equality $\pi_{\hat{\cal D}}\circ z_{G}=y_{\cal D}\circ \pi_{\cal D}'$ in light of Theorems \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism} and \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}. It is clear that $z_{G}$ is full and faithful, so it remains to show that it is $\widetilde{\hat{K}}$-dense. But this easily follows from the fact that every presheaf on $\cal D$ is $\hat{K}$-covered by representables.
nodes.statement_short: From $\pi_{\hat{\cal D}}\circ z_G=y_{\cal D}\circ\pi'_{\cal D}$; density since presheaves are covered by representables.
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Let us define the unit $\eta$ and counit $\epsilon$ of the dual adjunction. Given a morphism of sites $F:({\cal C}, J)\to ({\cal D}, K)$, the corresponding comorphism of sites $c_{F}:((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})\to ({\cal C}, J)$ is given by the canonical projection functor $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)\to {\cal C}$. The morphism of sites associated with $c_{F}$ is \[ m_{c_{F}}:({\cal C}, J)\to (\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}}), \] where $m_{c_{F}}(c)=\textup{Hom}_{\cal C}(c_{F}(-), c)$ (for any $c\in {\cal C}$).
nodes.statement_short: Plan; recall $c_F$ and its associated morphism $m_{c_F}$.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Define $\xi_F=m_{\pi_{\cal D}}$, a morphism of sites
nodes.statement: Let us define $\xi_{F}:{\cal D}\to \widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}$ as the functor sending any object $d\in {\cal D}$ to the presheaf $\textup{Hom}_{\cal D}(\pi_{\cal D}(-), d)$, where $\pi_{\cal D}$ is the canonical projection functor $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)\to {\cal D}$, and acting on the arrows in the obvious way. The functor $\xi_{F}$ yields a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to (\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}})$, since it is precisely the morphism of sites $m_{\pi_{\cal D}}$ associated as in Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}(iii) with the comorphism of sites $\pi_{\cal D}:((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})\to ({\cal D}, K)$ (note that $\pi_{\cal D}$ is indeed a comorphism of such sites by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii)).
nodes.statement_short: Define $\xi_F=m_{\pi_{\cal D}}$, a morphism of sites.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Show ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ{\bf Sh}(\xi_F)\cong{\bf Sh}(m_{c_F})$
nodes.statement: Let us check that, whilst \emph{not} necessarily commuting at the level of morphisms of sites, the diagram \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} ({\cal C}, J) \arrow[rr, "m_{c_{F}}"] \arrow[drr, "F"] & & (\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \hat{\tilde{K}}) \\ & & ({\cal D}, K) \ar[u, "\xi_{F}"] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} {\flushleft commutes after applying the functor ${\bf Sh}$ to it, i.e. ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})$.} Since $C_{y_{{\cal D}'}}:{\bf Sh}((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})\to {\bf Sh}(\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}})$ is an equivalence (cf. Proposition \ref{propyonedamorcomor}), to show that ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})$ it is equivalent to prove that ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}} \cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}$. Now, by Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}(iii), ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}={\bf Sh}(m_{\pi_{\cal D}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}} \cong C_{\pi_{\cal D}}$ and ${\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}\cong C_{c_{F}}$. But ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ C_{\pi_{\cal D}}\cong C_{c_{F}}$ by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii), as required.
nodes.statement_short: Show ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ{\bf Sh}(\xi_F)\cong{\bf Sh}(m_{c_F})$.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Reduce by precomposing with the equivalence $C_y$
nodes.statement: Since $C_{y_{{\cal D}'}}:{\bf Sh}((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})\to {\bf Sh}(\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}})$ is an equivalence (cf. Proposition \ref{propyonedamorcomor}), to show that ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})$ it is equivalent to prove that ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}} \cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce by precomposing with the equivalence $C_y$.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Rewrite both sides via Theorem 3.18(iii)
nodes.statement: Now, by Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}(iii), ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}={\bf Sh}(m_{\pi_{\cal D}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}} \cong C_{\pi_{\cal D}}$ and ${\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}\cong C_{c_{F}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite both sides via Theorem 3.18(iii).
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Conclude by Theorem 3.16(ii)
nodes.statement: But ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ C_{\pi_{\cal D}}\cong C_{c_{F}}$ by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii), as required.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by Theorem 3.16(ii).
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: ${\bf Sh}(\xi_F)$ is an equivalence
nodes.statement: The morphism ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F}):{\bf Sh}(\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}})\to {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)$ is actually an equivalence. Indeed, by Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}(iii), ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})={\bf Sh}(m_{c_{\pi_{\cal D}}})$ is an equivalence if and only if $C_{c_{\pi_{\cal D}}}$ is, and by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii), $C_{c_{\pi_{\cal D}}}$ is an equivalence if and only if ${\bf Sh}(\pi_{\cal D})$ is, which is the case by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii). We set the component $\epsilon_{F}:m_{c_{F}} \to F$ at $F$ of the counit $\epsilon$ of our adjunction equal to the geometric morphism ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})$ (note that this is actually an arrow $F\to m_{c_{F}}$ in ${\textup{\bf Mor}}_{({\cal C}, J)}$, that is, an arrow $m_{c_{F}} \to F$ in $({\textup{\bf Mor}}_{({\cal C}, J)})^{\textup{op}}$).
nodes.statement_short: ${\bf Sh}(\xi_F)$ is an equivalence; define the counit component.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Define the unit component $C_{\chi_G}$, an equivalence since $\chi_G=z_G\circ j_
nodes.statement: Let us now define the unit of our dual adjunction. Let $G$ be a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to ({\cal C}, J)$. The comorphism of sites $c_{m_{G}}:((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}})\to ({\cal C}, J)$ associated with the morphism of sites $m_{G}:({\cal C}, J)\to (\hat{D}, \hat{K})$ via Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(iii) is given by the canonical projection functor $(1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}) \to {\cal C}$. We define the component $\eta_{G}:G\to c_{m_{G}}$ of the unit at $G$ as the geometric morphism \[ C_{\chi_{G}}:{\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)\to {\bf Sh}((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}}) \] induced by the comorphism of sites \[ \chi_{G}:({\cal D}, K)\to ((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}}) \] given by the functor ${\cal D}\to (1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G})$ sending any object $d$ of $\cal D$ to the object $(y_{\cal D}(d), G(c), \alpha:y_{\cal D}(d)\to m_{G}(G(d))$, where $\alpha$ is the natural transformation corresponding to the identity on $G(d)$, regarded as an element of $m_{G}(G(d))(d)$, via the Yoneda lemma. Notice that $\chi_{G}$ is indeed a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to ((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}})$, since $\chi_{G}=z_{G}\circ j_{G}$, where $j_{G}$ and $z_{G}$ are the comorphisms of sites considered in Theorem \ref{thmtoposadjunction}(ii). Moreover, $C_{\chi_{G}}$ is an equivalence, since, by that theorem, both $C_{j_{G}}$ and $C_{z_{G}}$ are.
nodes.statement_short: Define the unit component $C_{\chi_G}$, an equivalence since $\chi_G=z_G\circ j_G$.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: The triangle of comorphisms commutes on the nose
nodes.statement: The diagram \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} ({\cal D}, K) \arrow[rr, "G"] \ar[d, "\chi_{G}"] & & ({\cal C}, J) \\ ((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}}) \ar[urr, "c_{m_{G}}"{below, xshift=1.5ex}] & & \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} {\flushleft of comorphisms of sites clearly commutes (without the need of applying the functor $C$ to it).}
nodes.statement_short: The triangle of comorphisms commutes on the nose.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Triangular identities follow from the commuting diagrams
nodes.statement: The verification that the unit and counit satisfy the triangular identities is an immediate consequence of their definition in light of the commutativity of the diagrams in Theorems \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism} and \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}; the details are straightforward and left to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Triangular identities follow from the commuting diagrams.
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Adjunction and comorphism properties of $i'_F$, $\pi^F_{\cal D}$
nodes.statement: (i) The fact that $\pi_{\cal D}^{F} \dashv i_{F}'$ is clear. By definition of coinduced topology $K^{i_{F}'}$, $i_{F}'$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'})$, which is also cover-preserving ($i_{F}'$ being full). So, by Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(i), its left adjoint $\pi_{\cal D}^{F}$ is a comorphism of sites $((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'}) \to ({\cal D}, K)$ and $i_{F}'$ is a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'})$. It remains to show that $\pi_{\cal C}^{F}$ is a comorphism of sites ${\bf Sh}((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'}) \to ({\cal C}, J)$. Let $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ be an object of $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$, and let us suppose that $R$ is a $J$-covering sieve on the object $c=\pi_{\cal C}^{F}((c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d)))$. Let $\tilde{R}$ be the sieve in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ on $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ generated by by the arrows of the form $(f, 1_{d}):(\textup{dom}(f), d, \alpha\circ f:\textup{dom}(f) \to F(d))\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$. Clearly, the image of $\tilde{R}$ under $\pi_{\cal C}^{F}$ is contained in $R$, so if we show that $\tilde{R}$ is $K^{i_{F}'}$-covering, we are done. Now, $\tilde{R}$ is $K^{i_{F}'}$-covering if and only if for any arrow $\xi=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})$ in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ to $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ from an object of the form $i_{F}'(d')=(F(d'),d', 1_{F(d')})$, $\xi^{\ast}(\tilde{R})$ contains the image under $i_{F}'$ of a $K$-covering sieve on $d'$. Notice that, since $\xi=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})$ is an arrow $(F(d'),d', 1_{F(d')})\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$, we have $\alpha\circ \xi_{1}=F(\xi_{2})$. Consider the sieve $\xi_{1}^{\ast}(R)$ on $F(d')$; it is $J$-covering as it is the pullback of a $J$-covering sieve. So, since $F$ is, by our hypothesis, a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to ({\cal C}, J)$, there is a $K$-covering sieve $T$ on $d'$ such that $F(T)\subseteq \xi_{1}^{\ast}(R)$. Let us show that $i_{F}'(T)\subseteq \xi^{\ast}(\tilde{R})$. For any $t\in T$, $\xi\circ i_{F}'(t)=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})\circ (F(t), t)=(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)),\textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}) \to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$. But $\xi_{1}\circ F(t)\in R$ and hence the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), 1_{d}):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t): F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ lies in $\tilde{R}$. But the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ can be written as the composite of this arrow with the arrow $(1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}, \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), \textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))})\to (F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t):F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))$, which is indeed an arrow in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ since $F(\xi_{2}\circ t)=\alpha \circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t)$ (this follows from the previously remarked fact that $\alpha\circ \xi_{1}=F(\xi_{2})$). So $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ also lies in $\tilde{R}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Adjunction and comorphism properties of $i'_F$, $\pi^F_{\cal D}$; covering lifting for $\pi^F_{\cal C}$ via an explicit sieve $\tilde R$.
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Fullness and density, then Proposition 5.5
nodes.statement: (ii) To show that $i_{F}'$ induces equivalences in the statement of the theorem, by Proposition \ref{propmorphismcomorphismequivalence} we are reduced, in light of (i), to prove that it is $K$-full and $K^{i_{F}'}$-dense. The functor $i_{F}'$ is actually full, so \emph{a fortiori} $K$-full, and it is $K^{i_{F}'}$-dense by Proposition \ref{propimagetopology}.
nodes.statement_short: Fullness and density, then Proposition 5.5.
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: From Theorem 3.13
nodes.statement: (i) This is an immediate consequence of Theorem \ref{thmfibration1}.
nodes.statement_short: From Theorem 3.13.
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Pullback lemma on the diagram of subtoposes
nodes.statement: (ii) This follows from the ($2$-dimensional) pullback lemma, which implies that the left-hand square in the following diagram (where the unnamed vertical arrows are the canonical geometric inclusions) is a pullback (since the right-hand square and the outer rectangle are): $$ \xymatrix{ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{J}_{F}) \ar[d] \ar[r] & {\bf Sh}((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), M^{\pi^{F}_{\cal C}}_{J}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[d]^{C_{F}} \\ [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{C_{i_{F}'}\quad} & [(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{\quad C_{\pi^{F}_{\cal C}}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] } $$ (notice that the composite of the lower horizontal arrows is $C_{F}$).
nodes.statement_short: Pullback lemma on the diagram of subtoposes.
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: From (ii) and Theorem 3.7
nodes.statement: (iii) This follows from (ii) and Theorem \ref{thmcorrespondenceinclusion}.
nodes.statement_short: From (ii) and Theorem 3.7.
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Faithfulness makes the counit epimorphic
nodes.statement: (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii). Since $R$ is faithful, for any object $e$ of $\cal E$, the component $\epsilon_{e}:L(R(e))\to e$ of the counit of the adjunction $L\dashv R$ is an epimorphism. So condition (ii) is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Faithfulness makes the counit epimorphic.

nodes.name: Epimorphisms from $L(u)$ factor through the counit, which is then epic
nodes.statement: (ii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i). Any arrow $\alpha:L(u)\to e$, $\alpha$ factors through the component $\epsilon_{e}$ at $e$ of counit of the adjunction $L\dashv R$. So if $\alpha:L(u)\to e$ is an epimorphism, $\epsilon_{e}$ is also an epimorphism. Since this holds for every $e$, it implies that $R$ is faithful.
nodes.statement_short: Epimorphisms from $L(u)$ factor through the counit, which is then epic.

nodes.name: Reduce to separating sets using that $L$ preserves epimorphic families
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the last assertion of the proposition. The fact that it suffices to require condition (ii) for every $e$ in $\cal C$ follows from the fact that every object $e$ of $\cal E$ admits an epimorphic family from objects in $\cal C$. On the other hand, since $\cal D$ is separating for $\cal F$, requiring, for a given object $c$, that there should be an epimorphism $L(u)\to c$, is equivalent to the condition that the family of all arrows $L(d)\to c$ (where $d\in {\cal D}$) is epimorphic (since $L$ preserves colimits, having a right adjoint, and hence epimorphic families).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to separating sets using that $L$ preserves epimorphic families.

nodes.name: Trivial implications
nodes.statement: The implications (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii) and (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (iii) are clear. The fact that, in (iii), if the factorization exists then it is unique (up to isomorphism) can be proved as follows.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial implications; announce uniqueness argument.

nodes.name: A factorization $r$ of $f^*$ preserves colimits, so has a right adjoint $j$
nodes.statement: Since $i^{\ast}\circ i_{\ast}\cong 1_{\cal F}$ and $i^{\ast}$ preserves colimits, if $f^{\ast}$ factors as $r\circ i^{\ast}$ then the functor $r$ preserves colimits and hence has a right adjoint; let us call it $j$.
nodes.statement_short: A factorization $r$ of $f^*$ preserves colimits, so has a right adjoint $j$.

nodes.name: Passing to right adjoints, $f_*\cong i_*\circ j$, giving (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i)
nodes.statement: Now, since $f^{\ast}\cong r\circ i^{\ast}$, passing to the right adjoints we obtain that $f_{\ast}\cong i_{\ast}\circ j$; in other words, $f_{\ast}$ factors (necessarily uniquely up to isomorphism) through $i_{\ast}$ and $j$ identifies with this factorization. So $r$ is uniquely determined as the left adjoint to this factorization. This argument actually proves that (iii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i). Similarly, we can prove that (ii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i).
nodes.statement_short: Passing to right adjoints, $f_*\cong i_*\circ j$, giving (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i); (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) similarly.

nodes.name: Unfold the definition via $R_{l'\circ A}$
nodes.statement: By definition, $A$ is $(J, K)$-continuous if and only if the functor \[ R_{l'\circ A}:{\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)\to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \] takes values in ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\subseteq [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold the definition via $R_{l'\circ A}$.

nodes.name: $R_{l'\circ A}\cong D_A\circ i_K$ by Yoneda, which gives the claim
nodes.statement: But we have \[ R_{l'\circ A} \cong D_{A}\circ i_{K}. \] Indeed, for any $E\in {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)$, \[ R_{l'\circ A}(E)= \textup{Hom}_{{\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)}((l'\circ A)(-), E)\cong E\circ A^{\textup{op}}=(D_{A}\circ i_{K})(E) \] naturally in $E$. From this our thesis immediately follows.
nodes.statement_short: $R_{l'\circ A}\cong D_A\circ i_K$ by Yoneda, which gives the claim.

nodes.name: The sheaf condition for the $R_A(e)$ is the colimit condition
nodes.statement: (i) and (ii) are immediate, since stating that all the functors of the form $R_{A}(e)=\textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(A(-), e)$ (for $e\in {\cal E}$) satisfy the sheaf condition with respect to a sieve $S$ on an object $c$ amounts precisely to saying that $A(c)=\varinjlim_{f:d\to c \in S} A(d)$.
nodes.statement_short: The sheaf condition for the $R_A(e)$ is the colimit condition.

nodes.name: The colimit condition gives epimorphic families
nodes.statement: (iii) The equality $A(c)=\varinjlim_{f:d\to c \in S} A(d)$ implies in particular that the family of arrows $\{A(\textup{dom}(f)) \to A(c) \mid f\in S\}$ is epimorphic, i.e. that $A$ is $J$-continuous. If $A$ is flat then the geometric morphism $(L_{A}\dashv R_{A})$ factors through the canonical inclusion ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ if and only if $A$ is $J$-continuous (see, for instance, Corollary 4 at p. 394 of \cite{MM}). The second assertion, about morphisms of sites, follows from the first about flat functors by Remark \ref{remmorphismsofsites}(a).
nodes.statement_short: The colimit condition gives epimorphic families; flat case by Mac Lane-Moerdijk.

nodes.name: Largest topology for which a class of presheaves are sheaves
nodes.statement: (iv) This follows from the fact that, for any collection $\cal P$ of presheaves on a given category $\cal C$, there is a largest Grothendieck topology for which all of them are sheaves. This topology can be explicitly characterized as the topology having as covering sieves precisely the sieves $S$ such that every presheaf $P$ in $\cal P$ satisfies the sheaf condition with respect to all the pullback sieves $g^{\ast}(S)$ (see, for instance, the proof of Proposition C2.1.9 \cite{El}). If $\cal P$ is the class of presheaves in the image of the functor $R_{A}$ then this condition amounts precisely to requiring that for any arrow $g:d\to c$, $A(d)=\varinjlim_{h:e\to d \in g^{\ast}(S)} A(e)$ (cf. the proof of (i)).
nodes.statement_short: Largest topology for which a class of presheaves are sheaves.

nodes.name: $A\mapsto(L_A\dashv R_A)$ and $f\mapsto f^*\circ y$ are quasi-inverse
nodes.statement: (i) One half of the equivalence is given by the assignment $A \mapsto (L_{A}\dashv R_{A})$; the other half sends a weak morphism $f$ to the functor $f^{\ast}\circ y_{\cal C}$. The two correspondences are quasi-inverses to each other since, on the one hand, for any functor $A:{\cal C}\to {\cal E}$, $L_{A}\circ y_{\cal C}\cong A$ and, on the other hand, for any weak morphism $f:{\cal E}\to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, $f^{\ast}\cong L_{f^{\ast}\circ y_{\cal C}}$ since both functors preserve arbitrary colimits (as they have right adjoints) and their composites with the Yoneda embedding are isomorphic to the same functor (namely, $f^{\ast}\circ y_{\cal C}$).
nodes.statement_short: $A\mapsto(L_A\dashv R_A)$ and $f\mapsto f^*\circ y$ are quasi-inverse.

nodes.name: Continuous functors give weak morphisms into sheaves and conversely
nodes.statement: (ii) If $A$ is $J$-continuous then $R_{A}$ factors through the canonical inclusion ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$. Regarded as a functor ${\cal E}\to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$, it preserves arbitrary limits (since ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ is closed in $[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ under arbitrary limits), so it has a left adjoint and hence defines a weak morphism of toposes $g:{\cal E}\to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ which, composed with the canonical geometric inclusion $i_{J}:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, gives the weak morphism induced by $A$; in particular, the inverse image $g^{\ast}:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$ of this morphism satisfies $g^{\ast}\circ a_{J}\cong L_{A}$. This also shows that the functor $A$ corresponding to $i_{J}\circ g$ is given by $g^{\ast}\circ l$; indeed, $A\cong L_{A}\circ y_{\cal C}\cong g^{\ast}\circ a_{J}\circ y_{\cal C}\cong g^{\ast}\circ l$. Conversely, given a weak morphism $f:{\cal E}\to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ corresponding as in (i) to a functor $A:{\cal C}\to {\cal E}$ (so that $f^{\ast}\cong L_{A}$ and $f_{\ast}\cong R_{A}$), if $f$ factors through ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ then $f_{\ast}$ (that is, $R_{A}$) factors through the direct image of the geometric inclusion ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, that is, $A$ is $J$-continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous functors give weak morphisms into sheaves and conversely.

nodes.name: List the four claims to be proved
nodes.statement: We have to prove that: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item For any $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $A:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$, the geometric morphism $C_{A}$ it induces is essential. \item For any essential geometric morphism ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$, the functor $f_{!}\circ l$ is a $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$. \item Any essential geometric morphism $f:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$ is equal to $C_{f_{!}\circ l}$. \item Any $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $A:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$ satisfies $A\cong (C_{A})_{!}\circ l$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: List the four claims to be proved.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $R_A$ is the inverse image of $C_A$, so $C_A$ is essential
nodes.statement: (i) By Proposition \ref{propweakmorphismequivalence}(ii), $A$ induces a pair of adjoint functors $L_{A} \dashv R_{A}$, where $R_{A}$ is the functor ${\cal E} \to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ given by: $e\mapsto \textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(A(-), e)$. Now, $R_{A}$ corresponds to the inverse image of the geometric morphism $C_{A}$ induced by $A$ under the equivalence ${\cal E}\simeq {\bf Sh}({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$; indeed, by Theorem 4 at p. 412 of \cite{MM}, $C_{A}^{\ast}(P)\cong a_{J}(P\circ A^{\textup{op}})$ for any $P\in {\bf Sh}({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$, whence, by taking $P=\textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(-, e)$, $C_{A}^{\ast}(\textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(-, e))\cong R_{A}(e)$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: $R_A$ is the inverse image of $C_A$, so $C_A$ is essential.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $f_!\circ l$ is continuous and has the covering lifting property
nodes.statement: (ii) Any essential geometric morphism of sites induces an adjunction $(f_{!}\dashv f^{\ast})$; so, by Proposition \ref{propweakmorphismequivalence}(ii), the functor $f_{!}\circ l$ is $J$-continuous. It remains to prove that $f_{!}\circ l$ is a $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$. Since $f_{!}$ has a right adjoint, namely $f^{\ast}$, which preserves covers, it satisfies the covering lifting property; from this it immediately follows that $f_{!}\circ l$ also satisfies the covering lifting property.
nodes.statement_short: $f_!\circ l$ is continuous and has the covering lifting property.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Compare essential images on representables
nodes.statement: (iii) By (ii), $f_{!}\circ l$ is a $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$. So, by (i), the geometric morphism $C_{f_{!}\circ l}$ it induces is essential. To show that $f\cong C_{f_{!}\circ l}$, it thus suffices to show that the essential images of the two geometric morphisms are isomorphic. Now, we saw in the proof of (i) that the essential image $u$ of $C_{f_{!}\circ l}$ satisfies the relation $u\circ a_{J}\cong L_{f_{!}\circ l}$, while the essential image of $f$ is $f_{!}$. In order to prove that $f_{!}\cong L_{f_{!}\circ l}\circ a_{J}$, since both functors are colimit-preserving, it is equivalent to show that they give isomorphic functors when composed with $l$. But $u\circ l=u\circ a_{J}\circ y_{\cal C}\cong L_{f_{!}\circ l} \circ y_{\cal C}\cong f_{!}\circ l$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Compare essential images on representables.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $A\cong(C_A)_!\circ l$ by comparing induced weak morphisms and (iii)
nodes.statement: (iv) By Proposition \ref{propweakmorphismequivalence}(ii), $A:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$ satisfies $A\cong (C_{A})_{!}\circ l$ if and only if $A$ and $(C_{A})_{!}\circ l$ induce the same weak morphisms ${\cal E}\to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$. Now, since $A$ and $(C_{A})_{!}\circ l$ are both $J$-continuous comorphisms of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$ (the latter by (i), which ensures that $C_{A}$ is essential, and then by (ii)), by the proof of (i) the inverse image of the weak morphism induced by $A$ is $(C_{A})_{!}$ and the inverse image of the weak morphism induced by $(C_{A})_{!}\circ l$ is $(C_{(C_{A})_{!}\circ l})_{!}$. But (iii) ensures that for any essential geometric morphism $f:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$, $f\cong C_{f_{!}\circ l}$, equivalently $f_{!}\cong (C_{f_{!}\circ l})_{!}$; applying this to $f=C_{A}$ thus yields our thesis.
nodes.statement_short: $A\cong(C_A)_!\circ l$ by comparing induced weak morphisms and (iii).
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $D_A$ restricts to sheaves
nodes.statement: (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii). By Proposition \ref{propequivGroth}, $D_{A}$ restricts to a functor ${\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K) \to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$. Then the following diagram commutes: \[ \xymatrix{ [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{D_{A}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \\ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K) \ar@{^{(}->}[u]_{i_{K}} \ar[r]^{(C_{A})^{\ast}} & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J). \ar@{^{(}->}[u]^{i_{J}} } \] Indeed, $(C_{A})^{\ast}$ is given, by definition, by the functor $a_{J}\circ D_{A}\circ i_{K}$; so, if $D_{A}\circ i_{K}$ takes values in ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ then $i_{J}\circ (C_{A})^{\ast}\cong D_{A}\circ i_{K}$. Taking the left adjoints to all the functors in the above square (notice that $C_{A}$ is essential by Theorem \ref{thmequivalencecomorphisms}, since $A$ is $J$-continuous, equivalently satisfies condition (ii)) thus yields an isomorphism $a_{K}\circ \textup{Lan}_{A^{\textup{op}}} \cong (C_{A})_{!}\circ a_{J}$; in particular, $a_{K}\circ \textup{Lan}_{A^{\textup{op}}}$ factors through $a_{J}$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: $D_A$ restricts to sheaves; take left adjoints of the square.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: (ii) is equivalent to (i), which implies (iii)
nodes.statement: (ii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (iii) We first notice that, by the compatibility of adjoints with respects to composition, condition (ii) is equivalent to condition (ii) of Proposition \ref{propequivGroth} and hence, by that proposition, to condition (i). But we have already observed, in the proof that (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii), that (i) actually implies (iii).
nodes.statement_short: (ii) is equivalent to (i), which implies (iii).
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Compose the square with Yoneda and apply Theorem 4.20
nodes.statement: (iii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i) By Theorem \ref{thmequivalencecomorphisms}, it suffices to show that $l'\circ A\cong (C_{A})_{!}\circ l$. But this immediately follows from the commutativity of the square in condition (iii), by composing both functors with $y_{\cal C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the square with Yoneda and apply Theorem 4.20.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $z_A$ is iso iff its restriction to representables is
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the last part of the corollary. We preliminarily note that, since both functors $(C_{A})_{!} \circ a_{J}$ and $a_{K}\circ \textup{Lan}_{A^{\textup{op}}}$ preserve arbitrary colimits, $z_{A}$ is an isomorphism if and only if $z_{A}y_{\cal C}:(C_{A})_{!}\circ l\to l'\circ A$ is. If $z_{A}y_{\cal C}$ is an isomorphism then $A$ is $J$-continuous by Theorem \ref{thmequivalencecomorphisms}. Conversely, if $A$ is $J$-continuous then, as we have proved above, condition (iv) is satisfied, with the isomorphism $(C_{A})_{!} \circ a_{J} \cong a_{K}\circ \textup{Lan}_{A^{\textup{op}}}$ being precisely $z_{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: $z_A$ is iso iff its restriction to representables is.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Identify the arrow with $\eta_P$ whiskered by $(F^{op})^*$
nodes.statement: Let $(F^{\textup{op}})^{\ast}$ be the functor $D_{F}:=(-\circ F^{\textup{op}}):[{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$. Then the arrow in the statement of the proposition is precisely $\eta_{P}(F^{\textup{op}})^{\ast}$, where $\eta_{P}:P\to a_{K}(P)$ is the component at $P$ of the unit of the adjunction between $a_{K}$ and the inclusion functor of $K$-sheaves into presheaves.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the arrow with $\eta_P$ whiskered by $(F^{op})^*$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: The comorphism square gives that $a_J$ inverts the arrow
nodes.statement: As we observed in section \ref{sec:presheaflifting}, since $F$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal D}, K)$, we have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ [{{\cal D}}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{D_{F}} \ar[d]_{a_{K}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[d]^{a_{J}} \\ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K) \ar[r]^{C_{F}^{\ast}} & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J). } \] From this it immediately follows that, since $\eta_{P}$ is sent by $a_{K}$ to an isomorphism, $a_{J}$ sends $\eta_{P}(F^{\textup{op}})^{\ast}$ to an isomorphism, as required.
nodes.statement_short: The comorphism square gives that $a_J$ inverts the arrow.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Then $a_K(P)\circ F^{op}$ is already a sheaf
nodes.statement: Now, if $F$ is $(J, K)$-continuous then, by Proposition \ref{propequivGroth}, the presheaf $a_{K}(P)\circ F^{\textup{op}}$ is already a $J$-sheaf, whence the final assertion of the proposition follows.
nodes.statement_short: Then $a_K(P)\circ F^{op}$ is already a sheaf.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $C_F$ is essential
nodes.statement: Since $F$ is continuous, by Corollary \ref{correstrictioncomorphism} the geometric morphism $C_{F}:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\to {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)$ is essential.
nodes.statement_short: $C_F$ is essential.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $C_{p^F_Q}$ is essential as a localization of $C_F$
nodes.statement: So, by Proposition \ref{proplocalizationcanonicalcomorphism}, the geometric morphism $C_{p^{F}_{Q}}$ induced by $p^{F}_{Q}$ is also essential, as it is (isomorphic to) a localisation of the essential geometric morphism $C_{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: $C_{p^F_Q}$ is essential as a localization of $C_F$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Reduce continuity to commutativity of a square
nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{correstrictioncomorphism}, we can prove that $p^{F}_{Q}$ is continuous by showing that the diagram $$ \xymatrix{ \int (Q\circ F^{\textup{op}}) \ar[r]^{\quad \quad p^{F}_{Q}\,} \ar[d]_{l_{\int (Q\circ F^{\textup{op}})}} &{\int Q} \ar[d]^{l_{\int Q}} \\ {\bf Sh}(\int (Q\circ F^{\textup{op}}), J_{Q\circ F^{\textup{op}}}) \ar[r]^{\quad\quad(C_{p^{F}_{Q}})_{!}} & {\bf Sh}(\int Q, J_{Q}) } $$ commutes.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce continuity to commutativity of a square.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Introduce the comparison cube
nodes.statement: Now, consider the following cube: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=small] & {\cal C} \arrow[dd, "l"{yshift=4ex}, rightarrow] \arrow[rr, "F"] & & {\cal D} \arrow[dd, "l'"{yshift=2ex}, rightarrow] \\ \int (Q\circ F^{\textup{op}}) \arrow[dd] \arrow[rr, "p^{F}_{Q}"{xshift=-4ex}, crossing over] \arrow[ru, "\pi_{Q\circ F^{\textup{op}}}"] & & {\int Q} \arrow[dd, crossing over] \arrow[ru, "\pi_{Q}"] & \\ & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \arrow[rr, "(C_{F})_{!}\quad\quad"{below, xshift=-3ex}] & & {\bf Sh}({\int Q}, J_{Q}) \\ {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\slash C_{F}^{\ast}(a_{K}(Q)) \arrow[ru, "V_{C_{F}^{\ast}(a_{K}(Q))}"'] \arrow[rr, "(C_{F}\slash a_{K}(Q))_{!}"'] & & {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)\slash a_{K}(Q) \arrow[ru, "V_{a_{K}(Q)}"'] & \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where $V_{a_{K}(Q)}$ and $V_{C_{F}^{\ast}(a_{K}(Q))}$ are obvious forgetful functors and the vertical unnamed arrows are the canonical ones modulo the equivalences of Proposition \ref{proplocalizationcanonicalcomorphism}.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the comparison cube.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: The frontal face commutes since the other faces do and $V_{a_K(Q)}$ reflects iso
nodes.statement: In light of the Proposition, we have to prove that the frontal face of the cube commutes. But this follows from the fact that the functor $V_{a_{K}(Q)}$ reflects isomorphisms, since the top face of the cube commutes by definition of $p^{F}_{Q}$, the lateral faces commute by Example \ref{examplemorphismsofdiscretefibrations}, the bottom face commutes since the square consisting of the right adjoints of the given functors clearly commutes, and the back face commutes by Corollary \ref{correstrictioncomorphism} as by our hypothesis $F$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: The frontal face commutes since the other faces do and $V_{a_K(Q)}$ reflects isos.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Restricting $g_!\dashv g^*$ to representables gives $F\dashv G$, $F$ continuous
nodes.statement: (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii) Suppose that $g={\bf Sh}(G)$ is essential. Let us denote by $F$ the restriction of $g_{!}$ to the representables. We know from Corollary \ref{correstrictioncomorphism} that $F$ is $(J, K)$-continuous. It thus remains to prove that $F\dashv G$. But this follows from the fact that $g_{!}\dashv g^{\ast}$, since $F$ is the restriction of $g_{!}$ to the representables and $G$ is the restriction of $g^{\ast}$ to the representables.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting $g_!\dashv g^*$ to representables gives $F\dashv G$, $F$ continuous.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $C_F={\bf Sh}(G)$, essential by Corollary 4.23
nodes.statement: (ii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i) By Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(iv), $C_{F}= {\bf Sh}(G)$. Since $F$ is $(J, K)$-continuous then, by Corollary \ref{correstrictioncomorphism}, $C_{F}={\bf Sh}(G)$ is essential and its essential image restricts to the representables, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: $C_F={\bf Sh}(G)$, essential by Corollary 4.23.
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Fix $f$ and a $P$-compact object $a$
nodes.statement: Let $f:{\cal F}\to {\cal E}$ be an essential geometric morphism and $a$ a $P$-compact object of $\cal F$. We want to prove that $f_{!}(a)$ is $P$-compact.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $f$ and a $P$-compact object $a$.

nodes.name: Pull the family back along the unit to get an epimorphic family on $a$
nodes.statement: Let $\{e_{i}:u_{i}\to f_{!}(a) \mid i\in I\}$ be an epimorphic family to $f_{!}(a)$. Then the family $\{f^{\ast}(e_{i}):f^{\ast}(u_{i})\to f^{\ast}(f_{!}(a)) \mid i\in I\}$ is also epimorphic, and so is its pullback along the unit arrow $\eta_{a}:a\to f^{\ast}(f_{!}(a))$. In other words, given the pullbacks \[ \xymatrix{ c_{i} \ar[r]^{\xi_{i}} \ar[d]_{s_{i}} & a \ar[d]^{\eta_{a}} \\ f^{\ast}(u_{i}) \ar[r]^{f^{\ast}(e_{i})} & f^{\ast}(f_{!}(a)) } \] the family $\{\xi_{i}:c_{i}\to a\}$ is epimorphic.
nodes.statement_short: Pull the family back along the unit to get an epimorphic family on $a$.

nodes.name: Refine it by a $P$-family and push forward by $f_!$
nodes.statement: Since $a$ is $P$-compact, there is an epimorphic family of arrows $\{\chi_{k}:b_{k}\to a \mid k\in K\}$ satisfying $P$ and, for each $k$ an index $i_{k}$ and a factorization $\xi_{i_{k}}\circ z_{k}$ of $\chi_{k}$ through $\xi_{i_{k}}$. Therefore the image $\{f_{!}(\chi_{k}):f_{!}(b_{k})\to f_{!}(a) \mid k\in K\}$ under $f_{!}$ of this family is epimorphic (since $f_{!}$ preserves colimits) and satisfies $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Refine it by a $P$-family and push forward by $f_!$.

nodes.name: Check the refinement by transposition along $f_!\dashv f^*$
nodes.statement: It remains to show that this family refines $\{e_{i}:u_{i}\to f_{!}(a) \mid i\in I\}$. For each $k\in K$, let $w_{k}$ be the arrow $s_{i_{k}}\circ z_{k}:b_{k}\to f^{\ast}(u_{i_{k}})$, and $\overline{w_{k}}:f_{!}(b_{k})\to u_{i_{k}}$ be its transpose along the adjunction $f_{!}\dashv f^{\ast}$. Let us show that, for each $k\in K$, $f_{!}(\chi_{k})=e_{i_{k}}\circ \overline{w_{k}}$; this will establish our thesis. By applying $f^{\ast}$ to both sides and composing the obtained arrow with the unit $\eta_{b_{k}}:b_{k}\to f^{\ast}(f_{!}(b_{k}))$, our equality rewrites as $f^{\ast}(f_{!}(\chi_{k}))\circ \eta_{b_{k}} = f^{\ast}(e_{i_{k}}\circ \overline{w_{k}})\circ \eta_{b_{k}}$. But $f^{\ast}(f_{!}(\chi_{k}))\circ \eta_{b_{k}}=\eta_{a}\circ \chi_{k}$, while $f^{\ast}(e_{i_{k}}\circ \overline{w_{k}})\circ \eta_{b_{k}}=f^{\ast}(e_{i_{k}})\circ f^{\ast}(\overline{w_{k}})\circ \eta_{b_{k}}=f^{\ast}(e_{i_{k}})\circ w_{k}=f^{\ast}(e_{i_{k}}) \circ s_{i_{k}}\circ z_{k}=\eta_{a}\circ \xi_{i_{k}}\circ z_{k}=\eta_{a}\circ \chi_{k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check the refinement by transposition along $f_!\dashv f^*$.

nodes.name: The induced topology is subcanonical
nodes.statement: (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (iii) This follows from the fact that $J_{\cal E}^{\textup{can}}|_{\cal C}$ is subcanonical and hence contained in the canonical topology on $\cal C$.
nodes.statement_short: The induced topology is subcanonical.

nodes.name: Trivial
nodes.statement: (iii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii) This is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial.

nodes.name: The colimit in $\cal E$ lies in $\cal C$, so $\overline S$ is epimorphic
nodes.statement: (ii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i) If $S$ is effective-epimorphic in $\cal C$ then $c$ is the colimit of $D_{S}$ in $\cal C$. Now, since the colimit of $D_{\overline{S}}$ in $\cal E$ lies in $\cal C$ by our hypothesis, it necessarily yields a colimit of $D_{S}$ in $\cal C$ and hence it coincides with $c$. Indeed, since $\cal C$ is separating for $\cal E$, any cone over $D_{S}$ in $\cal C$ can be uniquely extended to a cone over $D_{\overline{S}}$ in $\cal E$ (with the same vertex). So $\overline{S}$ is epimorphic in $\cal E$, that is, $S\in J_{\cal E}^{\textup{can}}|_{\cal C}(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: The colimit in $\cal E$ lies in $\cal C$, so $\overline S$ is epimorphic.

nodes.name: Covering sieves are universally effective-epimorphic and contain $P$-families by
nodes.statement: Since the topology $J^{c}_{P}$ is subcanonical, it is contained in the canonical topology on ${\cal E}^{c}_{P}$. In particular, all its covering sieves are universally effective-epimorphic. To show that every $J^{c}_{P}$-covering sieve contains a family of arrows to $c$ which satisfies $P$ and which is universally effective-epimorphic, it suffices to prove that every $J^{c}_{P}$-covering sieve contains a $J^{c}_{P}$-covering family which satisfies property $P$. But this follows at once from the $P$-compactness of $c$.
nodes.statement_short: Covering sieves are universally effective-epimorphic and contain $P$-families by $P$-compactness.

nodes.name: Reduce via Lemma 4.35 to showing the colimit $e$ is $P$-compact
nodes.statement: Conversely, we want to show that if a sieve $S$ on an object $c$ of ${\cal E}^{c}_{P}$ contains a family of arrows to $c$ which satisfies $P$ and which is effective-epimorphic then $S$ is $J^{c}_{P}$-covering. This will follow at once from Lemma \ref{lemmainducedcanonicaltopology} once we have proved that if $R$ is a sieve generated by a family of arrows $\{r_{i} \mid i\in I\}$ in ${\cal E}^{c}_{P}$ satisfying $P$ then the colimit $e$ in $\cal E$ of the diagram $D_{\overline{R}}$ lies in $\cal C$. We have to show that $e$ is $P$-compact. The universal property of the colimit yields colimit arrows $\{\lambda_{i}:\textup{dom}(r_i)\to E \mid i\in I\}$ and an arrow $\alpha:e\to c$ such that $\alpha \circ \lambda_{i}=r_{i}$ for each $i\in I$. By condition (3), the family $\{\lambda_{i}:\textup{dom}(r_i)\to e \mid i\in I\}$ satisfies property $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Lemma 4.35 to showing the colimit $e$ is $P$-compact.

nodes.name: Refine pullbacks of $\cal F$ and multicompose, using fractality
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal F}$ be an epimorphic family on $e$, which can suppose to be a sieve without loss of generality. We want to prove that it admits an epimorphic refinement satisfying $P$. For each $i\in I$, the family $\lambda_{i}^{\ast}({\cal F})$ is epimorphic on ${\rm dom}(r_i)$. Since ${\rm dom}(r_i)$ is $P$-compact, $\lambda_{i}^{\ast}({\cal F})$ is refined by an epimorphic family of arrows ${\cal F}_{i}$ to $\textup{dom}(r_{i})$ satisfying $P$. So the multicomposite family $\{\lambda_i \mid i\in I\} \ast \{{\cal F}_{i} \mid i\in I\}$ satisfies $P$ (since $P$ is fractal). Since this family is also epimorphic (notice that the family $\{\lambda_i \mid i\in I\}$ is epimorphic by the universal property of the colimit) and clearly refines $\cal F$, our thesis is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Refine pullbacks of $\cal F$ and multicompose, using fractality.

nodes.name: Relate conditions (3) and (4)
nodes.statement: By the above arguments, if conditions (1) and (2) are satisfied, then condition (3) implies condition (4). Conversely, (4) implies (3). Indeed, if ${\cal R}=\{r_i:{\rm dom}(r_i) \to c \mid i\in I\}$ is such a family then the family of canonical colimit arrows $\{\lambda_i:{\rm dom}(r_i) \to e \mid i\in I\}$ corresponds to $\cal R$ under the identification $e\cong c$ and hence \emph{a fortiori} satisfies $P$ since $\cal R$ does.
nodes.statement_short: Relate conditions (3) and (4).

nodes.name: Conditions (1) and (4) suffice by Lemma 4.35
nodes.statement: On the other hand, conditions (1) and (4) alone ensure, by Lemma \ref{lemmainducedcanonicaltopology}, that if a sieve $S$ on an object $c$ of ${\cal E}^{c}_{P}$ contains a family of arrows to $c$ which satisfies $P$ and which is effective-epimorphic then $S$ is $J^{c}_{P}$-covering, so they allow to conclude the thesis of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (1) and (4) suffice by Lemma 4.35.

nodes.name: Pullback stability and heredity give condition (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, let us show that if $P$ is stable under pullback and hereditary then condition (3) is satisfied. Consider the pullbacks $s_{i}$ of the arrows $r_{i}$ along $\alpha:e\to c$. By the universal property of the pullback, there is a unique arrow $m_{i}:{\rm dom}(r_i)\to u_i$ such that $s_i\circ m_i=\lambda_i$ and $t_i\circ m_i=1_{{\rm dom}(r_i)}$: \[ \begin{tikzcd} {\rm dom}(r_i) \ar[ddr, "\lambda_{i}"', bend right] \ar[dr, "m_{i}"description]\ar[drr, "1_{{\rm dom}(r_i)}", bend left]&&\\ &u_{i} \ar[d, "s_{i}"] \ar[r, "t_{i}"] & \textup{dom}(r_i) \ar[d, "r_i"] \\ & e \ar[r, "\alpha"']& c \ar[ul, "\lrcorner"{xshift=-1.5ex, yshift=0.5ex, near end}, phantom] \end{tikzcd} \] It follows in particular that $m_i$ is a (split) monomorphism (for each $i\in I$). Since $P$ is stable under pullback and $\{r_{i} \mid i\in I\}$ satisfies $P$, the family ${\cal S}:=\{s_i \mid i\in I\}$ also satisfies $P$. Then, the fact that $P$ is hereditary implies that the family $\{\lambda_i \mid i\in I\}$ also satisfies $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Pullback stability and heredity give condition (3).

nodes.name: Pull back the $r_i$ along $\alpha$
nodes.statement: Consider the pullbacks $s_{i}$ of the arrows $r_{i}$ along $\alpha:e\to c$. By the universal property of the pullback, there is a unique arrow $m_{i}:{\rm dom}(r_i)\to u_i$ such that $s_i\circ m_i=\lambda_i$ and $t_i\circ m_i=1_{{\rm dom}(r_i)}$: \[ \begin{tikzcd} {\rm dom}(r_i) \ar[ddr, "\lambda_{i}"', bend right] \ar[dr, "m_{i}"description]\ar[drr, "1_{{\rm dom}(r_i)}", bend left]&&\\ &u_{i} \ar[d, "s_{i}"] \ar[r, "t_{i}"] & \textup{dom}(r_i) \ar[d, "r_i"] \\ & e \ar[r, "\alpha"']& c \ar[ul, "\lrcorner"{xshift=-1.5ex, yshift=0.5ex, near end}, phantom] \end{tikzcd} \] It follows in particular that $m_i$ is a (split) monomorphism (for each $i\in I$).
nodes.statement_short: Pull back the $r_i$ along $\alpha$; the induced $m_i$ are split monos.

nodes.name: Stability gives $P$ for the $s_i$, heredity for the $\lambda_i$
nodes.statement: Since $P$ is stable under pullback and $\{r_{i} \mid i\in I\}$ satisfies $P$, the family ${\cal S}:=\{s_i \mid i\in I\}$ also satisfies $P$. Then, the fact that $P$ is hereditary implies that the family $\{\lambda_i \mid i\in I\}$ also satisfies $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Stability gives $P$ for the $s_i$, heredity for the $\lambda_i$.

nodes.name: Explicit left adjoint via the counit of $f_!\dashv f^*$
nodes.statement: (i) It is easy to see that a left adjoint to $$f^{\ast}|_{\textup{Sub}_{\cal E}(A)}:\textup{Sub}_{\cal E}(A)\to \textup{Sub}_{\cal F}(f^{\ast}(A))$$ is given by $m\in \textup{Sub}_{\cal E}(A) \mapsto \textup{Im}(\epsilon_{A}\circ f_{!}(m))$, where $\epsilon_{A}:f_{!}(f^{\ast}(A))\to A$ is the component at $A$ of the counit of the adjunction $f_{!}\dashv f^{\ast}$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit left adjoint via the counit of $f_!\dashv f^*$.

nodes.name: By definition
nodes.statement: (ii) This is clear by definition of weakly essential geometric morphism.
nodes.statement_short: By definition.

nodes.name: Counterexample with $L=\mathbf 2$ and a locally connected non-connected $L'$
nodes.statement: (iii) Take $L=\textbf{2}=\{0,1\}$, $L'$ arbitrary and $u$ equal to the unique frame homomorphism $L \to L'$; then $u$ is clearly complete, and hence it has a left adjoint $L'\to 2$. By Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(i), this preorder map is therefore a comorphism of sites $(L', J^{\textup{can}}_{L'})\to (\textbf{2}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\textbf{2}})$, which induces the unique geometric morphism ${\bf Sh}(L')\to {\bf Sh}(\textbf{2}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\textbf{2}})\simeq {\bf Set }$. This comorphism sends $0$ to $0$ and any non-zero element of $L'$ to $1$. Now, if $L'$ is locally connected then this morphism is essential but if $L'$ is not connected then the essential image of this morphism sends the terminal object to the set of its connected components rather than to an element of $\textbf{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample with $L=\mathbf 2$ and a locally connected non-connected $L'$.

nodes.name: Counterexample with a non-locally connected $L'$
nodes.statement: (iv) Take $L=\textbf{2}=\{0,1\}$ and $L'$ to be any not locally connected locale and $u$ equal to the unique frame homomorphism $L \to L'$. Then $u$ is complete but the geometric morphism ${\bf Sh}(u):{\bf Sh}(L')\to {\bf Sh}(\textbf{2})\simeq {\bf Set }$ which it induces is not essential (cf. point (iii) above).
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample with a non-locally connected $L'$.

nodes.name: Via frames of ideals, the left adjoint restricts to a poset map inducing $f$
nodes.statement: (v) Let $f:{\cal F}\to {\cal E}$ be a weakly essential geometric morphism and ${\cal F}\simeq [{\cal Q}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, ${\cal E}\simeq [{\cal P}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, where $\cal P$ and $\cal Q$ are posets. Then ${\cal F}\simeq {\bf Sh}(\textup{Id}(\cal Q))$, ${\cal E}\simeq {\bf Sh}(\textup{Id}(\cal P))$, where $\textup{Id}(\cal P)$ and $\textup{Id}(\cal Q)$ are respectively the frame of ideals of $\cal P$ and of $\cal Q$. Indeed, these are exactly the frames of subterminal objects of $[{\cal P}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ and $[{\cal Q}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$. Therefore the geometric morphism $f$ is induced by a frame homorphism $n:\textup{Id}(\cal P)\to \textup{Id}(\cal Q)$, which is given by the restriction of its inverse image $f^{\ast}$ to subterminals. Since $f$ is by our hypothesis weakly essential, it thus follows $n$ admits a left adjoint. This implies that the left adjoint to $n$ restricts to a poset homomorphism $u:{\cal Q}\to {\cal P}$ (cf. the proof of Proposition \ref{proppreservationcompactness} below) and hence that $n$ can be identified with the frame homomorphism $\textup{Id}(u):\textup{Id}({\cal P}) \to \textup{Id}({\cal Q})$. So $f$ can be identified with the geometric morphism induced by $u$, since they have isomorphic inverse image functors; in particular, $f$ is essential, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Via frames of ideals, the left adjoint restricts to a poset map inducing $f$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\hat f$ being a comorphism
nodes.statement: The commutativity of the above diagram will follow from the functoriality of the geometric morphisms induced by comorphism of sites, once we have proved that $\hat{f}:([{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }], \hat{J}) \to ([{\cal C}'^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }], \hat{J'})$ is a comorphism of sites.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\hat f$ being a comorphism.

nodes.name: By Proposition 3.14(i), reduce to $D_f$ preserving covers
nodes.statement: Since $\hat{f}$ has a right adjoint, namely the inverse image functor $E(f)^{\ast}=D_{f}:=(-\circ f^{\textup{op}})$ of the essential geometric morphism $E(f):[{{\cal C}'}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ induced by $f$, it is equivalent to show that this latter functor sends $\hat{J'}$-covering families to $\hat{J}$-covering families (cf. Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(i)).
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 3.14(i), reduce to $D_f$ preserving covers.

nodes.name: The square $a_J\circ E(f)^*\cong C_f^*\circ a_{J'}$ shows $D_f$ preserves covers
nodes.statement: For this, we observe that, since $f$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J)\to ({\cal C}', J')$, the direct image of the geometric morphism $C_{f}$ induced by it is given by the restriction to sheaves of the direct image of $E(f)$; passing to the left adjoints, we obtain the commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ [{{\cal C}'}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{E(f)^{\ast}} \ar[d]_{a_{J'}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[d]^{a_{J}} \\ {\bf Sh}({\cal C}', J') \ar[r]^{C_{f}^{\ast}} & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J), } \] from which it immediately follows that $E(f)^{\ast}$ sends $\hat{J'}$-covering families to $\hat{J}$-covering families.
nodes.statement_short: The square $a_J\circ E(f)^*\cong C_f^*\circ a_{J'}$ shows $D_f$ preserves covers.

nodes.name: Comorphism property from the sheafification criterion
nodes.statement: Since a sieve $S$ on an object $c$ is $J$-covering if and only if it is sent by the associated sheaf functor $a_{J}$ to an isomorphism, $y_{\cal C}$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to (\hat{\cal C}, \hat{J})$.
nodes.statement_short: Comorphism property from the sheafification criterion.

nodes.name: Via the Comparison Lemma, $l\circ y$ corresponds to the flat continuous $a_J\cir
nodes.statement: To see that it is also a morphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to (\hat{\cal C}, \hat{J})$, we have to show that $l_{\hat{\cal C}}\circ y_{\cal C}$ is a $J$-continuous flat functor ${\cal C} \to {\bf Sh}(\hat{\cal C}, \hat{J})$. But the Comparison Lemma yields an equivalence \[ {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \simeq {\bf Sh}(\hat{\cal C}, \hat{J}), \] under which this functor corresponds precisely to the functor $a_{J}\circ y_{\cal C}$, which is clearly flat and $J$-continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Via the Comparison Lemma, $l\circ y$ corresponds to the flat continuous $a_J\circ y$.

nodes.name: Fullness and density since presheaves are colimits of representables
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $y_{\cal C}$ is $\hat{J}$-dense and $J$-full. But $y_{\cal C}$ is full and hence \emph{a fortiori} $J$-full, while the $\hat{J}$-denseness follows from the fact that every presheaf is a colimit of representables, whence it is $\hat{J}$-covered by them in $\hat{\cal C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fullness and density since presheaves are colimits of representables.

nodes.name: Apply the criterion of Proposition 4.13
nodes.statement: To show that $p:(M^{p}_{K}, {\cal C})\to ({\cal D}, K)$ is continuous, we shall apply the criterion of Proposition \ref{propcharcanonicalfunctors}. First, it is clear from the characterization of the topology $M^{p}_{K}$ given by Theorem \ref{thmfibration1} that $p$ is cover-preserving.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the criterion of Proposition 4.13; $p$ is cover-preserving by Theorem 3.13.

nodes.name: Remains: local connectedness of squares
nodes.statement: So it remains to prove that, given a $M^{p}_{K}$-covering sieve $S$ on an object $c$ and a commutative diagram of the form \[ \xymatrix{ d \ar[r]^{w} \ar[d]^{z} & p(c') \ar[d]^{p(f)} \\ p(c'') \ar[r]^{p(g)} & p(c), } \] where $f:c'\to c$ and $g:c''\to c$ are two arrows of $S$, there is a $K$-covering family $\{d_{i}\to d \mid i\in I\}$ such that for each $i\in I$, the composites $d_{i}\to p(c')$ and $d_{i}\to p(c'')$ belong to the same connected component of the category $(d_{i}\downarrow D^{p}_{S})$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains: local connectedness of squares.

nodes.name: Take the covering sieve $\chi^*(\langle p(P_S)\rangle)$
nodes.statement: Our $K$-covering family on $d$ will be given by the sieve $\chi^{\ast}(\langle p(P_{S})\rangle )$, where $P_{S}$ is the presieve consisting of the cartesian arrows in $S$ and $\chi$ is the arrow $p(f)\circ w=p(g)\circ z$ witnessing the commutativity of the above square. Notice that, by Theorem \ref{thmfibration1}, this sieve is indeed $K$-covering.
nodes.statement_short: Take the covering sieve $\chi^*(\langle p(P_S)\rangle)$.

nodes.name: Connect both arrows through a cartesian $\xi$ in $S$
nodes.statement: We have to check that, for any $\alpha\in \chi^{\ast}(\langle p(P_{S})\rangle )$, the arrows $w\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c')$ and $z\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c'')$, regarded as objects of the category $({\rm dom}(\alpha)\downarrow D^{p}_{S})$, belong to the same connected component. Since $\alpha\in \chi^{\ast}(\langle p(P_{S})\rangle )$, there is a cartesian arrow $\xi$ in $S$ and an arrow $\gamma$ such that $\chi\circ \alpha =p(\xi)\circ \gamma$. The arrow $\xi$ will actually serve as a means for connecting our two arrows; indeed, we will show that, on the one hand, $\gamma:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p({\rm dom}(\xi))$ and $w\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c')$ belong to the same connected component of $({\rm dom}(\alpha)\downarrow D^{p}_{S})$ and that, on the other hand, $\gamma:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p({\rm dom}(\xi))$ and $z\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c'')$ belong to the same connected component of $({\rm dom}(\alpha)\downarrow D^{p}_{S})$, from which it follows by transitivity that $w\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c')$ and $z\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c'')$ belong to the same connected component, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Connect both arrows through a cartesian $\xi$ in $S$.

nodes.name: Use the fibration property and cartesianness of $\xi$ to build the connecting zi
nodes.statement: To prove that $\gamma:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p({\rm dom}(\xi))$ and $w\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c')$ belong to the same connected component of $({\rm dom}(\alpha)\downarrow D^{p}_{S})$, we observe that, since $p$ is a fibration, there are an object $\tilde{c'}$ of $\cal C$, an isomorphism $\tau:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(\tilde{c'})$ and an arrow $h:\tilde{c'}\to c'$ such that $p(h)\circ \tau=w\circ \alpha$. Next, we notice that, since $\chi=p(f)\circ w$ and $\chi\circ \alpha =p(\xi)\circ \gamma$, we have $p(f)\circ w\circ \alpha=p(\xi)\circ \gamma$ and hence $p(f)\circ p(h)\circ \tau=p(\xi)\circ \gamma$, equivalently, $p(f\circ h)=p(\xi)\circ \gamma \circ \tau^{-1}$. From the fact that $\xi$ is cartesian, it thus follows that there is an arrow $\psi:\tilde{c'}\to {\rm dom}(\xi)$ such that $p(\psi)=\gamma\circ \tau^{-1}$ and $\xi\circ \psi=f\circ h$. We thus see from the following diagram that $\gamma$ and $w\circ \alpha$ belong to the same component of $({\rm dom}(\alpha)\downarrow D^{p}_{S})$ (where the vertical unnamed arrow is $p(f\circ h)=p(\xi\circ \psi)$): \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} & {\rm dom}(\alpha) \ar[d, "\tau"] \ar[ld, "\gamma"{above}] \ar[rd, "w\circ \alpha"] & \\ p({\rm dom}(\xi)) \ar[dr, "p(\xi)\quad"{below}] & p(\tilde{c'}) \ar[d] \ar[l, "p(\psi)"{above}] \ar[r, "p(h)"] & p(c') \ar[ld, "p(f)"] \\ & p(c) & \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Use the fibration property and cartesianness of $\xi$ to build the connecting zig-zag.

nodes.name: The other half is analogous
nodes.statement: The proof that $\gamma:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p({\rm dom}(\xi))$ and $z\circ \alpha:{\rm dom}(\alpha)\to p(c'')$ also belong to the same connected component of $({\rm dom}(\alpha)\downarrow D^{p}_{S})$ is completely analogous.
nodes.statement_short: The other half is analogous.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of fillers for cartesian arrows
nodes.statement: (i) This is an immediate consequence of the uniqueness of the filling arrow in the definition of cartesian arrow.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of fillers for cartesian arrows.

nodes.name: Functoriality from the universal property of cartesian arrows
nodes.statement: (ii) It is well-known that, since $C$ is a fibration, every arrow of $\cal D$ can be (uniquely up to unique isomorphism) factored as a vertical arrow followed by a cartesian arrow. It remains to show that this factorization is functorial. But this follows immediately from the universal property of cartesian arrows.
nodes.statement_short: Functoriality from the universal property of cartesian arrows.

nodes.name: Lift a zig-zag step by step using cartesianness and (i)
nodes.statement: (iii) The ` only if' direction is trivial, so we only have to show the converse one. So, let us suppose that $(f:c' \to c, C(\alpha):C(d)\to C(A(c')))$ and $(g:c''\to c, C(\beta):C(d)\to C(A(c'')))$ belong to the same connected component of the category $(C(d)\downarrow D^{C\circ A}_{S})$. Given a zig-zag connecting these two objects, we can obtain, by the functoriality of the factorizations of arrows in $S$, a zig-zag connecting the objects $(f_{c}:{\rm dom}(f_{c})\to c, C(A(f_{v})\circ \alpha):C(d)\to C(A({\rm dom}(f_{c}))))$ and $(g_{c}:{\rm dom}(g_{c})\to c, C(A(g_{v})\circ \beta):C(d)\to C(A({\rm dom}(g_{c}))))$, where the intermediate objects have the form $(h:{\rm dom}(h)\to c, u:C(d)\to C(A({\rm dom}(h))))$ for a cartesian arrow $h$ in $S$. Now, it is easy to see, by means of an inductive argument starting from one or the other of the two extremes of the zig-zag connecting $(f_{c}:{\rm dom}(f_{c})\to c, C(A(f_{v})\circ \alpha):C(d)\to C(A({\rm dom}(f_{c}))))$ and $(g_{c}:{\rm dom}(g_{c})\to c, C(A(g_{v})\circ \beta):C(d)\to C(A({\rm dom}(g_{c}))))$, by using the cartesianness of the arrows $h$, that each arrow $u$ is actually the image under $C$ of an arrow $\gamma:d\to A({\rm dom}(h))$ which makes the relevant triangle commute in the category $\cal D$. Indeed, suppose given two objects $(r:{\rm dom}(r)\to c, u:C(d')\to C(A({\rm dom}(r))))$ and $(s:{\rm dom}(s)\to c, v:C(d')\to C(A({\rm dom}(s))))$ of the category $(C(d')\downarrow D^{C\circ A}_{S})$, where the arrows $A(r)$ and $A(s)$ are cartesian, related by an arrow $t:{\rm dom}(s)\to {\rm dom}(r)$ in $\cal C$ such that $r\circ t=s$, in the sense the following diagram commutes: \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} & C(A({\rm dom}(r))) \ar[rd, "C(A(r))"] & \\ C(d') \ar[ur, "u"] \ar[dr, "v\quad"{below}] & & C(A(c)) \\ & C(A({\rm dom}(s))) \ar[uu, "\quad\quad\quad C(A(t))"{below}] \ar[ur, "\quad\quad\quad C(A(s))"{below}] & \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} If $v=C(\rho)$ for some arrow $\rho:d'\to A({\rm dom}(s))$ then $u=C(A(t))\circ v=C(A(t)\circ \rho)$ and the following diagram commutes: \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} & A({\rm dom}(r)) \ar[rd, "A(r)"] & \\ d' \ar[ur, "A(t)\circ \rho"] \ar[dr, "\rho\quad"{below}] & & A(c) \\ & A({\rm dom}(s)) \ar[uu, "\quad\quad A(t)"{below}] \ar[ur, "\quad\quad A(s)"{below}] & \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} If $u=C(\delta)$ for some arrow $\delta:d'\to A({\rm dom}(r))$ then, by the cartesiannes of the arrow $A(s)$ and part (i) of the lemma (applied to the cartesian arrow $A(r)$), there is a unique arrow $\rho:d'\to A({\rm dom}(s))$ such that $A(t)\circ \rho=\delta$. The following diagram thus commutes: \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} & A({\rm dom}(r)) \ar[rd, "A(r)"] & \\ d' \ar[ur, "\delta"] \ar[dr, "\rho\quad"{below}] & & A(c) \\ & A({\rm dom}(s)) \ar[uu, "\quad\quad A(t)"{below}] \ar[ur, "\quad\quad A(s)"{below}] & \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} So in both cases we have a lift of the connection between the objects $(r:{\rm dom}(r)\to c, u:C(d')\to C(A({\rm dom}(r))))$ and $(s:{\rm dom}(s)\to c, v:C(d')\to C(A({\rm dom}(s))))$ from the category $D^{C\circ A}_{S}$ to the category $D^{A}_{S}$. So our zig-zag can be lifted to a zig-zag connecting the objects $(f_{c}:{\rm dom}(f_{c})\to c, A(f_{v})\circ \alpha:d\to A({\rm dom}(f_{c})))$ and $(g_{c}:{\rm dom}(g_{c})\to c, A(g_{v})\circ \beta:d\to A({\rm dom}(g_{c})))$, and hence between the objects $(f:{\rm dom}(f_{c})\to c, \alpha:d\to A(c'))$ and $(g:c''\to c, \beta:d\to A(c''))$, since $(f_{c}:{\rm dom}(f_{c})\to c, A(f_{v})\circ \alpha:d\to A({\rm dom}(f_{c})))$ (resp. $(g_{c}:{\rm dom}(g_{c})\to c, A(g_{v})\circ \beta:d\to A({\rm dom}(g_{c})))$) is in the same connected component as $(f:{\rm dom}(f_{c})\to c, \alpha:d\to A(c'))$ (resp. $(g:c''\to c, \beta:d\to A(c''))$). The last statement of (iii) follows from (ii), since every morphism of fibrations sends cartesian arrows to cartesian arrows and vertical arrows to vertical arrows.
nodes.statement_short: Lift a zig-zag step by step using cartesianness and (i).

nodes.name: $S$ is generated by arrows with cartesian image
nodes.statement: The fact that $S$ admits a functorial statement as in the statement of the proposition implies that $S$ which is generated by a presieve $P$ of arrows $f$ such that $A(f)$ is cartesian (indeed, one can take $P$ to consist precisely of the arrows $g_{c}$ for $g\in S$).
nodes.statement_short: $S$ is generated by arrows with cartesian image.

nodes.name: $A(S)$ is $K$-covering
nodes.statement: Let us first prove that $A(S)$ is $K$-covering. From the existence of an isomorphism $C\circ A\cong B$ and the fact that $B$ is cover-preserving, it follows that the family $\{C(A(f))\mid f\in S\}$ is $L$-covering on $C(A(c))$. Now, since $C$ is a comorphism of sites, the sieve $S^{C}_{\langle \{C(A(f))\mid f\in S\}\rangle }$ is $K$-covering (we refer to section \ref{sec:smallestgrothendiecktopologycomorphism} for the notation). But by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(iii), since the presieve $\{A(f) \mid f\in P\}$ entirely consists of cartesian arrows, $S^{C}_{\langle \{C(A(f))\mid f\in S\}\rangle }=\langle \{A(f) \mid f\in P\}\rangle $; so $\langle \{A(f) \mid f\in P\}\rangle $ is $K$-covering, as required.
nodes.statement_short: $A(S)$ is $K$-covering.

nodes.name: $C(A(S))$ is $L$-covering
nodes.statement: From the existence of an isomorphism $C\circ A\cong B$ and the fact that $B$ is cover-preserving, it follows that the family $\{C(A(f))\mid f\in S\}$ is $L$-covering on $C(A(c))$.
nodes.statement_short: $C(A(S))$ is $L$-covering.

nodes.name: Covering lifting and Lemma 3.12(iii) give that $A(S)$ covers
nodes.statement: Now, since $C$ is a comorphism of sites, the sieve $S^{C}_{\langle \{C(A(f))\mid f\in S\}\rangle }$ is $K$-covering (we refer to section \ref{sec:smallestgrothendiecktopologycomorphism} for the notation). But by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(iii), since the presieve $\{A(f) \mid f\in P\}$ entirely consists of cartesian arrows, $S^{C}_{\langle \{C(A(f))\mid f\in S\}\rangle }=\langle \{A(f) \mid f\in P\}\rangle $; so $\langle \{A(f) \mid f\in P\}\rangle $ is $K$-covering, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Covering lifting and Lemma 3.12(iii) give that $A(S)$ covers.

nodes.name: Take a commutative square over two arrows of $S$
nodes.statement: Let us now suppose that we have a commutative square of the form \[ \xymatrix{ d \ar[r]^{\chi} \ar[d]^{\xi} & A(c') \ar[d]^{A(f)} \\ A(c'') \ar[r]^{A(g)} & A(c), } \] where $f,g\in S$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a commutative square over two arrows of $S$.

nodes.name: Continuity of $B$ connects the images locally
nodes.statement: Consider the image of this square under the functor $C$: using the isomorphism $C\circ A\cong B$, we obtain a commutative square \[ \xymatrix{ C(d) \ar[r] \ar[d] & B(c') \ar[d]^{B(f)} \\ B(c'') \ar[r]^{B(g)} & B(c). } \] The $(J, L)$-continuity of $B$ thus ensures the existence of a $L$-covering family $\{r_{i}:e_{i}\to C(d) \mid i\in I\}$ such that the composite arrows $e_{i}\to B(c')$ and $e_{i}\to B(c'')$ belong to the same connected component of the category $(e_{i} \downarrow D^{B}_{S})$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $B$ connects the images locally.

nodes.name: Lift the covering family along $C$
nodes.statement: Now, since $C$ is a comorphism of sites, there is a $K$-covering family $\{g_{k}:d_{z}\to d \mid z\in Z\}$ whose image under $C$ is contained in the sieve generated by the family $\{e_{i}\to C(d) \mid i\in I\}$. So for each $z\in Z$ there are an element $i_{z}\in I$ and an arrow $h_{z}:d_{z}\to e_{i_{z}}$ such that $r_{i_{z}}\circ h_{z}=C(g_{z})$
nodes.statement_short: Lift the covering family along $C$.

nodes.name: Lift connectedness via Lemma 4.45(iii)
nodes.statement: We thus have a commutative square \[ \xymatrix{ C(d_{z}) \ar[rr]^{C(\chi \circ g_{z})} \ar[d]^{C(\xi \circ g_{z})} & & C(A(c')) \ar[d]^{C(A(f))} \\ C(A(c'')) \ar[rr]^{C(A(g))} & & C(A(c)), } \] where the objects $C(\chi\circ g_{z})$ and $C(\xi \circ g_{z})$ belong to the same connected component of the category $(C(d_{z})\downarrow D^{C\circ A}_{S})$. Let us show that the objects $\chi\circ g_{z}$ and $\xi\circ g_{z}$ belong to the same connected component of the category $(d_{z}\downarrow D^{A}_{S})$. This will clearly imply our thesis. But this follows from the fact that, more generally, for any arrows $\alpha:d'\to A(c')$ and $\beta:d'\to A(c'')$ in $\cal D$ such that $C(\alpha)$ and $C(\beta)$ belong to the same connected component of the category $(C(d')\downarrow D^{C\circ A}_{S})$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ belong to the same connected component of the category $(d'\downarrow D^{C\circ A}_{S})$, which is an immediate consequence of Lemma \ref{lemmacartesianrelmono}(iii).
nodes.statement_short: Lift connectedness via Lemma 4.45(iii).

nodes.name: Proposition 4.46 applies to sieves closed under cartesian images
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemmacartesianrelmono}(iii) ensures that $H$ satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition \ref{propliftcontinuity} with respect to every sieve which contains all the cartesian images of its arrows (notice that a sieve has this property if and only if it is generated by a presieve entirely consisting of cartesian arrows).
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4.46 applies to sieves closed under cartesian images.

nodes.name: Reduce via the generators of $M^F_L$ and Proposition 4.11(iv)
nodes.statement: Now, not every $M^{F}_{L}$-covering sieve has this property, but $M^{F}_{L}$ is generated by sieves with this property. So, proving that $H$ is $(M^{F}_{L}, M^{G}_{L})$-continuous amounts precisely (by Proposition \ref{propcharJcanonical}(iv)) to showing that $H$ satisfies the continuity condition with respect to all the pullbacks of the sieves with the above property.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via the generators of $M^F_L$ and Proposition 4.11(iv).

nodes.name: Such sieves are closed under pullback (Lemma 3.12(vii))
nodes.statement: But by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(vii) this class of sieves is closed under pullback, whence our thesis follows.
nodes.statement_short: Such sieves are closed under pullback (Lemma 3.12(vii)).

nodes.name: All arrows are cartesian, so every sieve has the required factorization
nodes.statement: Since the canonical projection ${\cal D}\slash F(c)\to {\cal D}$ is a discrete fibration, all the arrows of ${\cal D}\slash F(c)$ are cartesian. Therefore every sieve $S$ in $\cal C$ trivially satisfies the property in Proposition \ref{propliftcontinuity}, namely that there is a functorial factorization $g=g_{c}\circ g_{v}$ for any arrow $g$ in $S$ such that $g_{c}$ lies in $S$, $A(g_{c})$ is a cartesian arrow and $A(g_{v})$ is a vertical arrow for \emph{any} functor $A:{\cal C}\to {\cal D}\slash F(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: All arrows are cartesian, so every sieve has the required factorization.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 4.46 with $A=F/c$
nodes.statement: Our thesis thus follows from the proposition by taking $A$ to be the functor $F\slash c$, and $B$ to be the composite of $F$ and the projection functor ${\cal C}\slash c \to {\cal C}$, and $C$ to be the projection functor ${\cal D}\to {\cal D}\slash F(c)$; note that $B$ is continuous as it is the composite of two continuous comorphisms of sites.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 4.46 with $A=F/c$.

nodes.name: Lift $G(g)$ along $F$ to a cartesian $f$
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha$ be an isomorphism $F\to G\circ H$. Given an arrow $g:d\to H(c)$ in $\cal D$, consider its image \[ G(g):G(d)\to G(H(c)) \] under $G$. Then its composite with $\alpha(c)^{-1}:G(H(c))\to F(c)$ yields an arrow $G(d)\to F(c)$ in $\cal E$. The fact that $F$ is a fibration implies that there is an isomorphism $\gamma:G(d)\to F(c')$ and a cartesian arrow $f:c'\to c$ such that $\alpha(c)^{-1}\circ G(g)=F(f)\circ \gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift $G(g)$ along $F$ to a cartesian $f$.

nodes.name: Lift $\gamma^{-1}$ along $G$
nodes.statement: Now consider the arrow \[ \gamma^{-1}:F(c')\to G(d). \] Since $G$ is a fibration, there are a cartesian arrow $k:d'\to d$ and an isomorphism $\beta:G(d')\to F(c')$ such that $\gamma^{-1}\circ \beta=G(k)$. Since $k$ is cartesian and $G(k)$ is an isomorphism, it follows that $k$ is an isomorphism. On the other hand, since $f$ is cartesian (with respect to $F$) and $H$ is a morphism of fibrations, the arrow $H(f):H(c')\to H(c)$ is cartesian (with respect to $G$). Now, we have \[ G(H(f))\circ (\alpha(c')\circ \beta)=G(g\circ k). \] Indeed, $G(H(f))\circ \alpha(c')\circ \beta=\alpha(c)\circ F(f)\circ \beta$ (by the naturality of $\alpha$), and $\alpha(c)\circ F(f)\circ \beta=G(g)\circ \gamma^{-1}\circ \beta=G(g)\circ G(k)=G(g\circ k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift $\gamma^{-1}$ along $G$; $k$ is an isomorphism and $H(f)$ is cartesian.

nodes.name: Factor $g$ through $H(f)$ with a vertical arrow
nodes.statement: So the cartesianness of $H(f)$ implies that there is a unique arrow $u:d'\to H(c')$ such that $H(f)\circ u=g\circ k$, equivalently $g=H(f)\circ (u\circ k^{-1})$. To conclude our proof, it remains to observe that the arrow $u\circ k^{-1}$ is vertical; but this follows from the fact that $G(u\circ k^{-1})=G(u)\circ G(k^{-1})=\alpha(c')\circ \beta \circ \beta^{-1} \circ \gamma=\alpha(c')\circ \gamma$, which is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $g$ through $H(f)$ with a vertical arrow.

nodes.name: Stack property: the square commutes iff the composite rectangles do
nodes.statement: (i) From the fact that the canonical indexing of a Grothendieck topos over itself is a stack with respect to the canonical topology it follows that the square \[ \xymatrix{ {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(B) \ar[rr]^{(f\slash B)_{!}} \ar[d]^{(f^{\ast}(h))^{\ast}} & & {\cal E}\slash B \ar[d]^{h^{\ast}} \\ {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(A) \ar[rr]^{(f\slash A)_{!}} & & {\cal E}\slash A } \] commutes if and only if each of the outer rectangles \[ \xymatrix{ {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(B) \ar[rr]^{(f\slash B)_{!}} \ar[d]^{(f^{\ast}(h))^{\ast}} & & {\cal E}\slash B \ar[d]^{h^{\ast}} \\ {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(A) \ar[rr]^{(f\slash A)_{!}} \ar[d]^{(f^{\ast}(f_{i}))^{\ast}} & & {\cal E}\slash A \ar[d]^{f_{i}^{\ast}}\\ {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(A_{i}) \ar[rr]^{(f\slash A_{i})_{!}} & & {\cal E}\slash A_{i} } \] does. But this rectangle is precisely the square corresponding to the arrow $h\circ f_{i}$. This shows that the commutativity of the square with respect to an arrow $h$ is equivalent to that of all the squares with respect to the arrows of the form $h\circ f_{i}$ for $i\in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Stack property: the square commutes iff the composite rectangles do.

nodes.name: Colimit-preserving functors agreeing on the $\Sigma_{c_k}$ agree
nodes.statement: (ii) Let us preliminarily notice that, for any epimorphic family $\{c_{k}:C_{k}\to C \mid k\in K\}$ in a Grothendieck topos $\cal E$, the family of functors $\{\Sigma^{\cal E}_{c_{k}}:{\cal E}\slash C_{k} \to {\cal E}\slash C\}$ satisfies the property that for any two colimit-preserving functors $H, K:{\cal E}\slash C \to {\cal F}$, there are isomorphisms $H\circ \Sigma^{\cal E}_{c_{k}}\cong K\circ \Sigma^{\cal E}_{c_{k}}$ satisfying the obvious coherence relations if and only if $H\cong K$. Indeed, for any object $[u:U\to C]$ of ${\cal E}\slash C$, consider the pullback squares \[ \xymatrix{ U_{k} \ar[rr]^{\xi_{k}} \ar[d]^{u_{k}} & & U \ar[d]^{u} \\ C_{k} \ar[rr]^{c_{k}} & & C. } \] Since the family $\{\xi_{k}:U_{k} \to U \mid k\in K\}$ is epimorphic, denoting by $S_{u}$ the sieve generated by the family $\{\xi_{k}:U_{k} \to U \mid k\in K\}$, we can represent $[u:U\to C]$ as the colimit in ${\cal E}\slash C$ of the diagram $D_{u}:{\int S}_{u}\to {\cal E}\slash C$ which sends any object $(Z, z:Z\to U)$ of ${\int S_{u}}$ to the object $[u\circ z:Z\to C]$ of ${\cal E}\slash C$. So, for any colimit-preserving functors $H$ and $K$ as above, $H([u])\cong K([u])$ if $H\circ D_{u}\cong K\circ D_{u}$. Now, we have such isomorphisms $H\circ D_{u}\cong K\circ D_{u}$ by the coherence relations existing by our hypotheses between the isomorphisms between the functors $H\circ \Sigma^{\cal E}_{c_{k}}$ and $K\circ \Sigma^{\cal E}_{c_{k}}$. Moreover, these isomorphisms $H([u])\cong K([u])$ (note that any object in the image of $D_{u}$ belongs to the image of some $\Sigma^{\cal E}_{c_{k}}$) are clearly natural in $[u:U\to C]\in {\cal E}\slash C$, which establishes our claim. Now, given, for each $j\in J$, the pullback square \[ \xymatrix{ A_{j} \ar[rr]^{h_{j}=g_{j}^{\ast}(h)} \ar[d]^{h^{\ast}(g_{j})} & & B_{j} \ar[d]^{g_{j}} \\ A \ar[rr]^{h} & & B, } \] consider the following cube: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=small] & {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(B) \arrow[dd, "(f^{\ast}(h))^{\ast}"{yshift=4ex}, rightarrow] \arrow[rr, "(f\slash B)_{!}"] & & {\cal E}\slash B \arrow[dd, "h^{\ast}"{yshift=2ex}, rightarrow] \\ {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(B_{j}) \arrow[dd, "(f^{\ast}(h_{j}))^{\ast}"{yshift=2.5ex, xshift=0ex}, rightarrow] \arrow[rr, "(f\slash B_{j})_{!}"{xshift=-4ex}, crossing over] \arrow[ru, "\Sigma^{\cal F}_{f^{\ast}(g_{j})}"] & & {\cal E}\slash B_{j} \arrow[dd, "h_{j}^{\ast}"{yshift=4ex}, rightarrow, crossing over] \arrow[ru, "\Sigma^{\cal E}_{g_{j}}"] & \\ & {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(A) \arrow[rr, "(f\slash A)_{!}"{below, xshift=-3ex}] & & {\cal E}\slash A \\ {\cal F}\slash f^{\ast}(A_{j}) \arrow[ru, "\Sigma^{\cal F}_{f^{\ast}(h^{\ast}(g_{j}))}"'] \arrow[rr, "(f\slash A_{j})_{!}"'] & & {\cal E}\slash A_{j} \arrow[ru, "\Sigma^{\cal E}_{h^{\ast}(g_{j})}"'] & \end{tikzcd} \end{center} We want to show that the back square is commutative (that is, $\Gamma^{f}_{h}$ holds) if and only if the front square is for each $j\in J$ (that is, if and only if $\Gamma^{f}_{g_{j}^{\ast}(h)}$ holds for each $j\in J$). This follows from the above preliminary remark and the fact that all the other squares in the cube commute. More specifically, the lower and upper squares commute since the squares obtained by taking the right adjoints of all functors commute, while the left-hand and right-hand lateral faces commute since they are commutative squares associated with local homeomorphisms of toposes (cf. Remark \ref{remlocallyconnectedcondition}).
nodes.statement_short: Colimit-preserving functors agreeing on the $\Sigma_{c_k}$ agree; conclude via a cube of slices.
